## Market Turmoil and Circuit Breakers

The Korean stock markets experienced a severe downturn today as geopolitical tensions in the Middle East triggered a global sell-off. The KOSPI index fell 5.72%, or 406.27 points, closing at 6690.62, while the KOSDAQ dropped 5.32%, losing 42.06 points to close at 740-level territory. Both markets activated sell-side circuit breakers simultaneously as foreign investors and institutions engaged in massive selling, with foreign investors alone dumping 5.7 trillion won worth of stocks. This marks the third "black day" for Korean markets this week, with sell-side circuit breakers triggering for the 66th time this year and circuit breakers for the 9th time. Notably, this week saw circuit breakers activate for five consecutive trading days, demonstrating extreme market volatility. The KOSPI had recovered above the 7000-point threshold just yesterday following a 4.04% surge, only to surrender those gains within a single trading session today.

## Oil Price Surge and Inflation Concerns

International crude oil prices spiked dramatically due to escalating Middle East tensions, reaching levels that triggered fresh inflation concerns in global markets. The surge in oil prices has led market participants to recalibrate expectations for continued interest rate hikes. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.7%, its highest level in approximately 18 months, reflecting market anxiety about persistent inflationary pressures. According to CME FedWatch data, the probability of a U.S. Federal Reserve rate hike in September now stands at 80.00%, up significantly from the previous week. October rate hike probability reached 87.00%, while December projections show 92.00% likelihood. Some analysts warn that if Middle East conflict escalates into a full-scale confrontation, crude oil prices could exceed 140 dollars per barrel, with some projections reaching as high as 146 dollars. The Korean government has maintained its oil price cap at current levels, citing the 3% inflation rate and existing pressures on ordinary household finances from higher interest rates.

## Housing Finance Policy Overhaul

The government announced comprehensive housing finance reforms that will be released shortly, following President Lee Jae-myeong's national housing policy forum on July 23rd. The financial authorities will implement differentiated property taxes targeting ultra-luxury homes and vacant single-property owners while providing tax relief for owner-occupied residences. The policy framework includes strengthening holding taxes on high-priced and speculative properties, significant reduction of capital gains tax benefits, and stricter regulation of jeonse loans for non-owner-occupied single properties. The government maintained its overall loan volume management stance while exploring targeted relaxation measures in specific sectors. These reforms represent a fundamental shift toward using taxation as the primary real estate policy tool, moving away from previous lending-based approaches.

## U.S. Tariff Pressures and Korean Exports

The Trump administration imposed 12.5% tariffs on Korea under the overcapacity provision, alongside tariffs on China and Japan at identical rates. Korean manufacturers across semiconductors, automobiles, steel, batteries, and machinery face significant headwinds from what analysts describe as overly broad and discretionary tariff applications. Notably, major export products including semiconductors, automobiles, and steel received temporary exemptions, though the tariff framework established under Section 301 remains as a latent threat. The government's blue house announced that Korea-U.S. agreements should preserve the 15.00% tariff ceiling and prevent additional tariff escalations through leveraging increased U.S. investment commitments. Battery manufacturers like LG Energy Solution face particular pressure as they source critical materials and minerals from China and other countries, raising production cost concerns.

## AI Partnership and Industrial Cooperation

President Lee met with major Korean technology executives including Samsung's Lee Jae-yong, SK's Chey Tae-won, and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang at the AI Summit on July 24th, establishing mega-scale partnerships in AI semiconductors and physical AI sectors. Korean companies including Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor, and Naver signed critical business agreements covering high-bandwidth memory and robotics technology with American big tech firms. This represents Korea and America's strategic response to China's rapid AI advancement, creating what analysts describe as a "mega-consortium" leveraging Korean manufacturing capabilities with American technological expertise. The collaboration includes physical AI deployment and associated labor policy initiatives to address potential employment disruptions. This partnership is expected to generate significant synergies in AI infrastructure development and next-generation industrial applications.

## Market Stabilization Measures

Financial authorities accelerated the implementation of enhanced deposit requirements for single-stock leverage products, raising minimum deposits for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix leverage ETFs and ETNs from 20 million won to 30 million won, effective July 31st. This expedited measure responds to President Lee's directive to implement stabilization measures more rapidly. SK Hynix leverage products have declined approximately 70.00% from their peak values, raising serious concerns about retail investor losses. The government signaled readiness to implement additional protective measures if market instability persists following these initial adjustments.

## Economic Outlook and Investor Implications

Today's market turmoil reflects converging global uncertainties: Middle East geopolitical risks, inflation resurgence threatening interest rate trajectories, and trade policy unpredictability from the Trump administration. For investors, today's sharp correction—with the KOSPI losing over 309 points from its opening position—underscores heightened volatility requiring careful risk management. The Korean real estate market faces structural headwinds from tightened financing conditions for speculative purchases, particularly affecting younger investors seeking property investments. Export-dependent sectors including semiconductors, automotive, and steel must navigate intensifying tariff environments while seeking strategic partnerships with American technology firms. International oil market volatility will likely persist given unresolved Middle East tensions, suggesting inflation management remains central to monetary policy discussions. The positive development of Korea-U.S. AI cooperation offers long-term growth opportunities in semiconductor and advanced manufacturing sectors, though near-term market weakness may create attractive entry points for patient investors with appropriate risk tolerance.
